paragraphs: The paper studies how to find small input changes that make ensembles of decision trees misclassify. These models behave like step functions, so the gradients used by many efficient attacks are unavailable. Attacks based only on the model's decisions remain possible, but they do not take advantage of how trees organize their predictions.

The authors reformulate the task as a discrete search over leaf tuples: combinations of leaves reached across the ensemble. The goal is to find a valid combination that produces a wrong prediction while remaining close to the original input. A greedy algorithm improves the candidate by exploring neighboring tuples that differ in one position.

Experiments cover large gradient boosting and random forest models with up to hundreds of trees. The method can be thousands of times faster than a mixed-integer programming approach and finds smaller perturbations than decision-based black-box attacks under the tested distance measures. These findings show the practical value of designing attacks around the model's discrete structure.
neurips-2020-an-efficient-adversarial-at.tldr: A discrete search over tree leaves produces fast, small adversarial perturbations for tree ensembles.

paragraphs: Federated learning distributes training across participants, creating opportunities to introduce backdoors that corrupt selected behaviors. This paper challenges the prospect of broadly reliable backdoor defenses through both theoretical results and a new attack family. Its concern is targeted failure on particular inputs, rather than simply lowering overall model performance.

The theoretical analysis establishes that, in the general case, robustness to backdoors implies robustness to adversarial examples. This connects backdoor defense to another major unresolved robustness problem. The authors also give reasons that detecting backdoors is unlikely under first-order oracle access or polynomial-time computation, making the computational setting central to the claim.

Their edge-case backdoors target seemingly straightforward inputs that occur in the tails of the data distribution and are unlikely to appear in training or testing. With careful adversarial tuning, the authors demonstrate insertion across image classification, optical character recognition, text prediction, and sentiment analysis while bypassing leading defenses. Such failures may have fairness consequences because rarely encountered inputs can be targeted even when routine evaluation misses them.
neurips-2020-attack-of-the-tails-yes-you.tldr: Theoretical obstacles and attacks on rare inputs expose serious challenges for defending federated learning against backdoors.

paragraphs: Coarse ranking asks a learner to divide uncertain options into ordered groups of predetermined sizes. Each option, or arm, produces observations from an unknown distribution. Every arm in an earlier group must have a higher mean than every arm in a later group, but the task does not require a complete ordering within each group.

The paper studies this problem when sampling policies can change only a small number of times. This batched restriction makes adaptability a resource: the learner must decide how much sampling to perform before revising its choices. The authors consider both a fixed sampling budget and a fixed confidence requirement, covering two different ways to specify the task.

They develop algorithms alongside impossibility results that nearly characterize the tradeoff between total arm pulls and policy changes. The lower bounds help establish how much room remains for improvement, while the algorithms show what is achievable. Experiments on real and synthetic data support their efficiency. The framework also encompasses simpler bandit tasks, including identifying the best arm.
neurips-2020-batched-coarse-ranking-in-m.tldr: The paper nearly characterizes how sampling effort trades off against policy changes when ranking bandit arms into ordered groups.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires solving a new task from very few labeled examples. Meta-learning approaches use experience with previous tasks to make this possible. This paper treats that process as a multilevel model and gives the task-specific inner learning step a Bayesian formulation through deep kernels.

The resulting method, Deep Kernel Transfer, learns a kernel that can carry useful information across tasks. The kernel supplies a learned way to relate examples, while the Bayesian treatment provides uncertainty estimates. The approach uses a single optimizer and avoids estimating task-specific parameters, simplifying the machinery required to learn from a small new dataset.

In the reported experiments, DKT beats several leading few-shot classification algorithms and achieves leading results for cross-domain adaptation and regression. These findings support the authors' conclusion that a simpler Bayesian model can replace complex meta-learning routines without losing accuracy in the evaluated settings. The contribution therefore combines predictive performance with a simpler learning procedure and an explicit treatment of uncertainty.
neurips-2020-bayesian-meta-learning-for-.tldr: Deep Kernel Transfer uses a simpler Bayesian meta-learning model to achieve strong few-shot results while quantifying uncertainty.

paragraphs: A classifier can assign high confidence to an input that belongs to none of its classes. This is especially troublesome when uncertainty should trigger human review or a safe operating state. The paper addresses whether low confidence on such out-of-distribution inputs can be protected against adversarial changes.

The training objective covers both an out-of-distribution example and a surrounding neighborhood defined by a maximum per-coordinate perturbation. Interval bound propagation computes an upper bound on the largest confidence anywhere in that neighborhood. Training minimizes this bound, so the objective addresses the worst case within the specified region rather than only the confidence at its center.

The authors show that meaningful confidence bounds can extend to out-of-distribution data beyond the examples used during training. They also find that certified worst-case detection can be achieved with little loss in classification accuracy. The guarantees concern confidence within the bounded neighborhoods, and the results demonstrate that this form of certification can have a modest accuracy cost.
neurips-2020-certifiably-adversarially-r.tldr: Training on certified confidence bounds enables robust out-of-distribution detection with little reported loss in classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Distributed matrix multiplication can be delayed by workers that finish slowly. This paper considers a sequence of jobs arriving in successive rounds, each with a deadline a fixed number of rounds later. That allowance creates an opportunity to organize redundant computation across time as well as across workers.

The authors propose two coding schemes that use this temporal flexibility. The first modifies polynomial coding without assuming a particular straggler model. For the same computational load per worker per round, it handles a broader collection of slow-worker patterns. The second assumes a specific straggler model and uses that additional structure to improve encoding and decoding complexity.

The theoretical results establish optimality for a particular class of straggler patterns and improved performance when stragglers are independent and identically distributed. Neural-network training experiments further validate the schemes. The central contribution is to show how a permitted delay between a job's arrival and deadline can become a useful resource for mitigating slow workers.
neurips-2020-coded-sequential-matrix-mul.tldr: Coding matrix multiplication across workers and time improves resilience to slow workers when jobs allow delayed completion.

paragraphs: Learned image compression often uses a variational autoencoder to turn an image into a latent representation that is easier to encode. Existing bits-back methods can approach a code length determined by the relative entropy between the latent posterior and prior. However, the methods discussed here require multiple images to reach their nominal efficiency and apply only to lossless compression.

The paper introduces Relative Entropy Coding, which directly encodes the latent representation. Its aim is to approach the same relative-entropy code length for an individual image. This changes the practical setting in which the efficiency can be useful: an image need not be compressed together with others to obtain the reported benefit.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet32, and Kodak support the single-image coding claim. REC also applies directly to lossy compression, where some image information may be discarded, and achieves competitive results on Kodak. The contribution connects efficient latent coding with both individual-image use and a broader compression setting.
neurips-2020-compressing-images-by-encod.tldr: Relative Entropy Coding efficiently encodes individual image latents and also supports competitive lossy compression.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with constraints asks an agent to pursue rewards while respecting additional requirements. This paper proposes an algorithm for the tabular episodic setting, where learning proceeds through episodes and the problem uses a table-based representation. Its focus is on broadening the kinds of objectives and constraints that can be treated with theoretical guarantees.

The analysis covers concave rewards together with convex constraints, as well as hard constraints described as knapsacks. These settings go beyond the linear constraints emphasized in much previous work. The authors also distinguish their scope from approaches centered on whether constraints can be satisfied at all or on problems involving only a single episode.

A modular analysis provides strong theoretical guarantees for these settings. Experiments in existing constrained episodic environments report substantial improvements over the compared approaches. Together, the analysis and experiments support the proposed algorithm as a way to address richer constrained learning problems, with the tabular episodic formulation defining the scope of the contribution.
neurips-2020-constrained-episodic-reinfo.tldr: A tabular episodic reinforcement-learning algorithm handles concave rewards, convex constraints, and hard knapsack constraints with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain generalization seeks a predictor that learns from several source domains and works in an unseen target domain. A common strategy makes feature distributions look alike across sources using an adversarial domain discriminator. The paper argues that this addresses only marginal distributions, leaving unresolved whether the features' relationship with class labels is consistent.

The authors add an entropy regularizer that measures dependence between learned features and labels. They combine it with the prediction loss and the adversarial domain-discrimination loss. This joins the goal of hiding domain differences with the need to retain a stable connection between features and the classes being predicted.

The paper gives a guarantee that its overall objective learns conditionally invariant features across the source domains. This is the property the authors identify as more relevant to prediction in new domains. Comparisons with leading methods on simulated and real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The findings support strengthening domain alignment with label-related structure to improve generalization.
neurips-2020-domain-generalization-via-e.tldr: An entropy regularizer strengthens domain alignment by enforcing conditional feature invariance across source domains.

paragraphs: Extragradient methods solve saddle-point problems by taking an exploratory step before making the actual update. This extra look ahead helps avoid convergence failures that can affect ordinary gradient descent and ascent. The paper examines what happens when those gradient calculations are stochastic, so the directions used by the algorithm contain noise.

The authors show that ordinary extragradient can lose its convergence behavior under stochastic gradients, even in simple bilinear problems. Their remedy gives the exploratory step and the final update different step sizes. Exploration proceeds on a more aggressive timescale, while the update changes the current solution more conservatively.

The analysis shows that this separation allows convergence with stochastic gradients and provides sharp convergence rates under an error-bound condition. That condition is part of the stated rate result. The contribution explains why adding an exploratory step alone may be insufficient in a noisy setting and shows how the relative scaling of exploration and updating can restore convergence.
neurips-2020-explore-aggressively-update.tldr: Using more aggressive exploration than updating restores stochastic extragradient convergence, with sharp rates under an error-bound condition.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the cost of choosing initial centers for k-means clustering. The widely used k-means++ approach combines ease of implementation, theoretical guarantees, and strong practical results, but its seeding procedure can be slow on large datasets. The research question is whether that initialization can be accelerated while preserving its quality guarantees.

The authors introduce a seeding algorithm based on rejection sampling with near-linear running time. They establish that it retains the same theoretical guarantees as k-means++ and improves earlier results on fast seeding. Thus, the claimed speed improvement comes with a formal connection to the quality assurances that make the original method attractive.

The empirical evaluation reports substantially faster execution than k-means++ and solutions of equivalent quality. The theoretical and experimental findings address complementary concerns: the analysis preserves the guarantee, while the experiments check whether speed and quality align in practice. The contribution makes a well-established clustering initialization more efficient without a reported sacrifice in solution quality.
neurips-2020-fast-and-accurate-k-means-v.tldr: A near-linear-time seeding algorithm preserves k-means++ guarantees and empirically achieves comparable quality with much faster execution.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the theoretical understanding of k-means++ and its parallel counterpart, k-means||. Both are popular algorithms for the classic k-means clustering problem. The contribution consists of new analyses of these existing algorithms, with the aim of explaining more convincingly why they work so well in practice.

The authors improve approximation guarantees, which characterize how an algorithm's solution quality compares with the ideal clustering objective. They also improve bicriteria approximation guarantees, which assess quality while permitting a relaxation of another part of the clustering requirement. Considering both forms provides more than one way to describe the algorithms' theoretical behavior.

These results strengthen the mathematical justification for widely used methods. Their significance lies in obtaining better guarantees for algorithms already valued for practical performance, bringing the analysis closer to that practical experience. The stated finding is an improvement in what can be proved about k-means++ and k-means||, rather than a claim that the analysis itself changes how those algorithms execute.
neurips-2020-improved-guarantees-for-k-m.tldr: New analyses strengthen approximation and bicriteria guarantees for k-means++ and k-means||.

paragraphs: Many dynamic systems contain interacting objects whose states evolve together. Learning that evolution becomes difficult when measurements arrive at uneven times and some objects are missing from individual observations. This paper addresses those conditions instead of requiring complete snapshots at regular intervals.

The proposed LG-ODE model assumes a known graph describing the system's structure. A graph neural network encoder uses the irregular, partial observations to infer initial states without supervision. A neural ordinary differential equation then models continuous evolution in a latent representation, allowing the model to learn both a compact representation of trajectories and the dynamics within that representation.

The continuous-time formulation fits the problem's uneven observation times, while the graph encoder incorporates structural relationships among objects. Experiments on motion capture, spring systems, and charged particles demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The results support combining graph-based inference with latent differential equations for partially observed systems, with knowledge of the underlying graph remaining an explicit part of the model's setup.
neurips-2020-learning-continuous-system-.tldr: LG-ODE combines graph-based state inference with continuous latent dynamics to learn from irregular, partial observations.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender chooses what information to disclose to influence a receiver acting in their own interest. Computing an optimal signaling scheme usually requires knowing the receiver's utility function. This paper relaxes that knowledge requirement by making persuasion a repeated online learning problem.

At each round, the receiver has an unknown type selected adversarially from a finite set. The sender chooses a signaling scheme and seeks performance close to the best scheme that could have been chosen with hindsight. The authors consider both full-information and partial-information versions, reflecting different amounts of feedback available during learning.

The paper first establishes a computational hardness result for the per-round work needed to achieve no regret. It then provides algorithms whose regret grows sublinearly with the number of rounds and polynomially with game parameters. Sublinear regret means the average gap to the hindsight benchmark shrinks over time. The results therefore address both learnability under unknown preferences and the computational difficulty accompanying that goal.
neurips-2020-online-bayesian-persuasion-.tldr: Online persuasion algorithms achieve sublinear regret against adversarially chosen receiver types, alongside a computational hardness result.

paragraphs: Diffusion MRI supports analysis of brain microstructure and reconstruction of white-matter pathways, but noise can interfere with those downstream tasks. Patch2Self introduces a self-supervised method for suppressing that noise. It learns from the volume being processed, using the entire volume to construct a denoiser tailored to that data.

The method takes advantage of the oversampled measurement space of diffusion MRI, called q-space. This supplies information for separating structure from noise without specifying an explicit model for either one. The learned denoiser is locally linear and full-rank, giving the approach a particular mathematical form while retaining its data-driven training procedure.

The authors evaluate Patch2Self on both real and simulated data, comparing it with other unsupervised methods. They report quantitative and qualitative improvements in microstructure modeling, fiber tracking through bundle coherency, and model estimation. These results connect denoising to the quality of subsequent analysis: the claimed benefit extends beyond cleaner-looking images to improvements in the uses of the diffusion measurements.
neurips-2020-patch2self-denoising-diffus.tldr: Patch2Self learns a diffusion-MRI denoiser from each volume and improves downstream analysis without explicit signal or noise models.

paragraphs: Most graph neural networks repeatedly combine information from neighboring vertices, then pool vertex representations into a representation of the whole graph. Although their inputs are graphs, the update rules are typically parameterized by fully connected layers. This paper proposes an architecture whose learned components include graphs themselves, aiming for greater transparency.

The Random Walk Graph Neural Network begins with a collection of trainable hidden graphs. A random walk kernel compares each input graph with those learned graphs to produce a representation. A fully connected network then turns that representation into an output. Because the kernel is differentiable, the hidden graphs and the remaining network can be trained together.

The learned graph comparisons provide a more direct structural view of the model's representation. The authors demonstrate transparency on synthetic datasets and evaluate prediction on graph-classification datasets, where performance is competitive. The findings support graph-shaped learned components as a viable alternative architecture that combines interpretable structure with useful predictive performance.
neurips-2020-random-walk-graph-neural-ne.tldr: RWNN learns hidden graphs and compares them with inputs through a differentiable random walk kernel.

paragraphs: Self-supervised pretraining can help models learn useful features before labeled training. This paper makes that stage aware of adversarial robustness by seeking representations that remain consistent under both ordinary data augmentations and adversarial perturbations. The motivation is that small input changes can otherwise cause large feature changes or alter predicted labels.

The proposed Adversarial Contrastive Learning builds on a framework that encourages agreement between differently augmented views. The authors explore ways to formulate this contrastive task while injecting adversarial changes. This brings robustness into representation learning itself and supports models that need relatively few labels during subsequent training.

The empirical evaluation reports consistent improvements over existing methods. On CIFAR-10, ACL improves robust accuracy by 2.99% and standard accuracy by 2.14% relative to the previous leading unsupervised robust pretraining approach. It also improves semi-supervised adversarial training when labeled examples are scarce. These findings support enforcing feature consistency during pretraining as a useful way to strengthen both robustness and label efficiency.
neurips-2020-robust-pre-training-by-adve.tldr: Adversarial Contrastive Learning improves robustness and label efficiency by stabilizing features during self-supervised pretraining.

paragraphs: Point completion reconstructs missing object geometry from a partial collection of three-dimensional points. Directly decoding a compressed feature representation can struggle with varied object structures and detailed surfaces. This paper introduces SK-PCN, which separates recovering the overall shape from reconstructing the surface.

Given a partial scan, the network first predicts a three-dimensional skeleton representing global structure. It then learns displacements from skeletal points to form the surface. A local adjustment stage merges the observed input points with the predictions to refine the result. This gives the original measurements a direct role in correcting the reconstructed surface.

The authors argue that separating structure estimation and surface reconstruction makes learning easier and helps recover surface detail. Their skeleton-based approach also better supports estimation of point normals, enabling full surface meshes as well as completed point clouds. Qualitative and quantitative experiments across several object categories report improvements over existing methods for both outputs, supporting the usefulness of this structured reconstruction process.
neurips-2020-skeleton-bridged-point-comp.tldr: SK-PCN completes partial 3D scans by predicting a skeleton, reconstructing its surface, and refining it with observed points.

paragraphs: A stationary kernel uses a consistent notion of similarity across the input space. That simplicity can become restrictive when a function is smooth in some regions and varies more sharply in others. This paper develops input-dependent transformations that let a standard stationary kernel adapt to such changing behavior.

Instead of transforming each input into a single point, the method transforms it into a conditional Gaussian measure. These input-dependent measures control the effective smoothness of the kernel. The construction uses sparse-spectrum Gaussian processes, permits closed-form solutions, and can be stacked to capture more complicated patterns.

The authors validate the method against related algorithms on synthetic and real datasets. They report strong efficiency in the number of parameters needed by the warping functions in both small- and large-data settings. The contribution offers an explicit way to build nonstationary behavior from a stationary kernel, with the learned transformations expressing where and how smoothness should change across the input space.
neurips-2020-sparse-spectrum-warped-inpu.tldr: Input-dependent Gaussian warpings let sparse-spectrum Gaussian processes learn changing smoothness with efficient parameter use.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained network on a small dataset risks overfitting to limited examples. This paper addresses the problem by changing batch normalization, a component that adjusts features using summary statistics. The proposed StochNorm makes the choice of normalization statistics itself part of the regularization process.

StochNorm has two branches: one normalizes using the current mini-batch statistics, and the other uses moving statistics. Training selects between these branches stochastically, discouraging dependence on a particular set of sample statistics. The authors describe this as architecture regularization. The moving-statistics branch also naturally incorporates statistics retained from pretraining, bringing additional prior information into fine-tuning.

Extensive experiments show that the method helps avoid overfitting when fine-tuning with small datasets. It can be inserted into modern convolutional network backbones and combined with other fine-tuning methods for stronger regularization. Its contribution is therefore both a new source of randomness during adaptation and a way to reuse more of what normalization layers learned before fine-tuning.
neurips-2020-stochastic-normalization-c3.tldr: StochNorm reduces fine-tuning overfitting by randomly switching between mini-batch and moving-statistics normalization.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions when evaluating a black-box function is expensive. It traditionally assumes that the region to search is already known. This paper addresses problems where that assumption fails, making the choice of where to search part of the optimization process.

The proposed algorithm expands and shifts its search region over successive iterations. A hyperharmonic series controls the expansion rate, providing a mathematical rule for how the region grows. The authors also introduce a variant designed to scale to high-dimensional problems, extending the approach beyond the initial algorithm's setting.

For both algorithms, the paper proves that cumulative regret grows sublinearly. This means the average accumulated shortfall decreases as the number of iterations increases under the theoretical result. Experiments on synthetic and real optimization tasks show improvements over leading methods for unknown search spaces. Together, the findings support controlled search-region adaptation as a way to retain theoretical progress guarantees while tackling uncertainty about the search boundaries.
neurips-2020-sub-linear-regret-bounds-fo.tldr: Bayesian optimization with controlled expansion and shifting of its search region achieves sublinear cumulative regret.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training uses a single gradient-based perturbation to reduce training cost, but robustness can collapse within one epoch. This paper investigates that catastrophic overfitting in FGSM training. It shows that a random preliminary step does not prevent the problem and that randomness mainly helps by reducing perturbation magnitude.

The failure does not require a deep or heavily overparameterized model. The authors show it can occur in a single convolutional layer with few filters, with even one filter capable of creating strong local nonlinearity. This local behavior explains why a single gradient-based step can become an unreliable basis for adversarial training.

The proposed GradAlign regularizer explicitly encourages gradients to align within the allowed perturbation region. The authors report that this prevents catastrophic overfitting and improves FGSM training outcomes. It also enables training with larger maximum-coordinate perturbations and narrows the gap to multi-step adversarial training. The contribution links a concrete local failure mechanism to a regularizer designed to address it.
neurips-2020-understanding-and-improving.tldr: GradAlign addresses catastrophic overfitting in fast adversarial training by encouraging locally aligned gradients.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers a model from a source domain to a target domain, but their categories may overlap only partly. Many approaches assume a particular overlap pattern is known in advance. This paper introduces DANCE to handle arbitrary category shifts without requiring that setting to be specified beforehand.

DANCE combines two mechanisms. Self-supervised neighborhood clustering learns structure from the target data, reducing reliance on source categories as the sole guide to useful features. Entropy-based alignment and rejection then determine whether target features should align with source categories or be treated as belonging to unknown categories.

This combination addresses both learning a useful target representation and deciding which target examples fit the source label space. Extensive experiments show improvements over baselines across open-set, open-partial, and partial adaptation settings. The results support a common approach across several category-overlap situations, with self-supervision supplying target-specific structure and entropy guiding the choice between alignment and rejection.
neurips-2020-universal-domain-adaptation.tldr: DANCE combines target-domain clustering with entropy-based alignment and rejection to adapt across unknown category overlap.

paragraphs: When objects overlap in a photograph, only part of an object's extent is visible. Amodal completion estimates the whole object, including the region hidden behind another object. This paper introduces AMODAL-VAE, a variational generative framework for that task, motivated by applications such as detection, tracking, planning, and scene editing.

The method trains without amodal labels that explicitly mark the hidden extent of objects. Instead, it uses widely available object instance masks. That training setup matters because it allows the model to learn completion without requiring the specialized annotations that directly describe the desired completed shape.

The authors demonstrate interactive tools for completing and erasing objects in photographs. Experiments on complex street scenes achieve leading amodal-mask completion performance and produce high-quality scene edits. In a user study, participants prefer the model's inferred completions to human-labeled ones. That preference is evidence about perceived completion quality in the study, complementing the reported mask-completion results and the editing demonstration.
neurips-2020-variational-amodal-object-c.tldr: AMODAL-VAE learns to complete occluded object masks without amodal training labels and supports interactive scene editing.

paragraphs: FolkDuet generates a countermelody alongside a Chinese folk melody in real time. The challenge is to learn both how two musical lines interact and how to preserve Chinese folk style when no Chinese folk duet dataset is available. The paper addresses this with reinforcement learning guided by two separately learned rewards.

An interaction reward learns counterpoint relationships from duets formed using the outer parts of Bach chorales. A style reward learns melodic patterns from single-line Chinese folk songs. Together, these rewards train the generator to produce a complementary line while retaining the intended melodic style, drawing different kinds of musical knowledge from different sources.

Generation takes place online, allowing interactive human-machine duet improvisation rather than requiring the complete melody in advance. Experiments report better subjective and objective results than the baselines. The contribution demonstrates how separate rewards for musical interaction and style can guide generation when examples of their desired combination are unavailable.
neurips-2020-when-counterpoint-meets-chi.tldr: FolkDuet combines rewards learned from Bach and Chinese folk melodies to generate interactive countermelodies without folk-duet training data.
